planting.note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; M9 is a fully dwarfing understock requiring permanent staking or trellising.

directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; M9 is a fully dwarfing understock requiring permanent staking or trellising. Selected at England's East Malling Research Station in the early twentieth century, it remains the benchmark fully dwarfing apple rootstock against which most modern rootstocks are compared, producing a small tree roughly 25-30 percent the size of a standard seedling tree that bears fruit remarkably early and heavily for its size. Its brittle, shallow root system anchors poorly and requires permanent staking or trellising for the life of the tree, and it demands consistently fertile, well-drained soil and regular irrigation to perform well, making it best suited to intensively managed high-density plantings rather than a low-maintenance home orchard. Graft a desired named apple variety onto young rootstock in late winter, provide permanent support, and expect an extremely compact, easy-to-harvest tree bearing within two to three years.

planting.note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; M26 is a semi-dwarfing understock that benefits from staking in its early years.

directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; M26 is a semi-dwarfing understock that benefits from staking in its early years. Another classic East Malling selection, it produces a semi-dwarf tree roughly 40-50 percent the size of a standard seedling tree, notably hardier and more cold-tolerant than M9 while still offering meaningful size control and precocious early fruiting, making it a popular choice for colder-climate home orchards wanting a manageable tree size. Its root system is sturdier than M9 but still benefits from staking for the first several years until the tree is well established, and it performs best in fertile, well-drained soil, showing some susceptibility to fire blight and collar rot in poorly drained sites. Graft a desired named apple variety onto young rootstock in late winter, stake for the first few years, and expect a compact, productive tree well suited to a small home orchard in a colder climate.

planting.note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; M7 is a semi-dwarfing understock that is largely self-supporting once established.

directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; M7 is a semi-dwarfing understock that is largely self-supporting once established. A long-standing East Malling selection producing a semi-dwarf tree roughly 50-60 percent the size of a standard seedling tree, it develops a sturdier, more self-supporting root system than the more fully dwarfing M9 and M26 rootstocks, generally needing staking only while young rather than for the tree's entire life. It has a tendency to produce root suckers that should be removed periodically, and it shows good tolerance of a range of soil types along with reasonably good cold hardiness, making it a reliable choice for a home orchard tree of moderate, easy-to-manage size. Graft a desired named apple variety onto young rootstock in late winter, remove root suckers as they appear, and expect a productive tree that needs only temporary staking while establishing.

planting.note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; EMLA 26 is a virus-free selection of M26 with the same semi-dwarfing size and staking needs.

directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; EMLA 26 is a virus-free selection of M26 with the same semi-dwarfing size and staking needs. Developed through the joint East Malling and Long Ashton research stations' virus-indexing program in England, this is a heat-treated, virus-free selection of the classic M26 semi-dwarfing rootstock, offering the same 40-50 percent size reduction, cold hardiness, and precocious early fruiting as standard M26 but with improved vigor and productivity thanks to the elimination of latent viruses that historically reduced older rootstock stock's performance. Its virus-free status has made the EMLA-prefixed rootstock selections the preferred commercial source for M-series rootstocks in North America since their introduction. Graft a desired named apple variety onto young rootstock in late winter, stake for the first few years as with standard M26, and expect a compact, vigorous, productive semi-dwarf tree.

common_name: OHxF 97 Pear Rootstock (Old Home x Farmingdale 97)

planting.note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired pear variety onto the young rootstock; OHxF 97 is a semi-dwarfing, fire blight-resistant understock, not grown for its own fruit.

directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired pear variety onto the young rootstock; OHxF 97 is a semi-dwarfing, fire blight-resistant understock, not grown for its own fruit. Bred from a cross of the fire blight-resistant Old Home pear and Farmingdale pear at what is now Oregon State University, this rootstock in the widely used OHxF series produces a semi-dwarf to semi-standard tree around 75-85 percent the size of a standard seedling pear tree, valued above all for outstanding resistance to fire blight, one of the most destructive diseases of pear in humid growing regions. Its combination of moderate size control, strong anchorage that needs no permanent staking, and disease resistance has made the OHxF series the standard modern choice for pear rootstocks in North America, largely displacing the fire blight-susceptible quince rootstocks used in parts of Europe. Graft a desired named pear variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and expect a sturdy, disease-resistant, moderately sized tree well suited to humid-climate pear growing.

planting.note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a compatible desired pear variety onto the young rootstock, using an interstem for varieties incompatible with quince; BA29 is a dwarfing understock, not grown for its own fruit.

directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a compatible desired pear variety onto the young rootstock, using an interstem for varieties incompatible with quince; BA29 is a dwarfing understock, not grown for its own fruit. A French quince selection long used as a dwarfing pear rootstock in European orchards, it produces a smaller, more precocious tree than seedling pear rootstocks, roughly 50-65 percent of standard size, though it is somewhat less cold-hardy and more prone to iron chlorosis on high-pH soils than the seedling and OHxF pear rootstocks more commonly used in North America. Because many pear varieties are graft-incompatible with quince, an interstem of a compatible pear variety such as Old Home is often bench-grafted between the quince rootstock and the desired scion variety. Graft or double-work a desired named pear variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and reserve this rootstock for milder climates and growers specifically wanting a smaller, earlier-bearing pear tree.

planting.note: Plant container-grown rootstock liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft or bud a desired mandarin, orange, or other citrus variety onto the young rootstock; Cleopatra mandarin is grown as a salt-tolerant understock, not for its own fruit.

directions: Plant container-grown rootstock liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft or bud a desired mandarin, orange, or other citrus variety onto the young rootstock; Cleopatra mandarin is grown as a salt-tolerant understock, not for its own fruit. A small-fruited, seedy mandarin of little value for fresh eating, it is instead prized as a citrus rootstock for its outstanding tolerance of saline and poorly drained soils, good compatibility with mandarin and mandarin hybrid scion varieties in particular, and production of high-quality fruit on the grafted variety, though it is notably slow to bring young trees into full production compared to faster rootstocks like trifoliate orange hybrids. Its salt tolerance has made it a valued rootstock choice in coastal and irrigation-salinity-prone citrus growing regions where other common rootstocks struggle. Graft a desired named citrus variety onto young rootstock, and be patient with the extended juvenile period before the tree reaches full bearing compared to more precocious rootstock choices.

planting.note: Plant container-grown rootstock liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft or bud a desired citrus variety onto the young rootstock; Volkamer lemon is a vigorous, cold-hardy understock widely used in Gulf Coast home citrus production.

directions: Plant container-grown rootstock liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft or bud a desired citrus variety onto the young rootstock; Volkamer lemon is a vigorous, cold-hardy understock widely used in Gulf Coast home citrus production. A vigorous, cold-hardy lemon relative of uncertain hybrid origin, its own fruit is coarse and of little culinary value, but it is highly valued as a rootstock for producing large, fast-growing, precocious, and productive trees with notably better cold tolerance than many other citrus rootstocks, making it a common choice for home citrus trees in the marginal-climate Gulf South. Its vigor and cold hardiness have made it especially popular for backyard citrus in Texas, Louisiana, and coastal areas of the Gulf Coast where winter cold snaps threaten less hardy rootstocks. Graft a desired named citrus variety onto young rootstock, and expect a large, fast-growing, heavily-bearing tree that will need ample permanent space.
